Content.Primitive: From this slight sketch the nature of Mr. _Collingwood's book will very readily be understood. If the plot "be not very original, hoys are not particularly stern critics on this head, and com- pensation more than enough is afforded by the vigorous treatment. In the thrilling effect of his story the author has been admirably aided by the illustrations of W. H. Overend, whose artistic efforts show great skill and a thorough conception of the situation. Our specimen shows the JFZying Cloud, manned by Ned, Miss Stanhope, and one of the-sailors escaping from the mutineers. Mutiny likewise forms _m, prominent feature in Mr. Frankfort Moore's story Under Hatches, though introduced after a different fashion. Strangely enough, too, the hero's Christian name is also Ned ; and throughout the story other slight points of resemblance occur. But the main narrative follows dissimilar lines. Edward _WooUthorpe, the hero, in endeavouring to save the life of a man from drowning, is himself washed out to sea, is rescued by one Dowden in a boat, and eventually finds a refuge on board a light-ship. During a tremendous storm the latter is run down by a large vessel, and it is only by clinging to the rigging ?* the latter that _ISTed escapes with his life. His new home is a convict-ship, bound for Australia; and, though he might possibly be transferred to another vessel, homeward bound, injuries received to his knee during the collision forbid his removal. From this point ensues a most absorbing series of adventures, which will thoroughly interest the reader. One of the convicts turns out to be a complete ruffian, while another just as emphatically proves his honest, manly nature. A mutiny takes place on board, and the captain is compelled to abandon the vessel. But all comes right at the finish; the honest convict's innocence _ist proved, the mutineers are punished through a wonderful dispensation of Providence, and Ned is restored to his home and father. The illustrations, which are of a much higher order than is usually to be found in books of this kind, are by A. Forestier.
